Domain: natural numbers ℕ (whether zero- or one-based) with the usual strict order >. Units: none. Conditions: ordinary first-order quantifiers; the alleged m must be a single natural number independent of n.

Verdict: invalid. The premise ∀n∈ℕ ∃m∈ℕ (m>n) is true: for each n, choose m=n+1. The conclusion ∃m∈ℕ ∀n∈ℕ (m>n) is false. If such an m existed, instantiating n=m would give m>m, impossible; equivalently, n=m+1 would give m>m+1. Thus ℕ is unbounded above and has no greatest element, but no natural number exceeds every natural number.

The defect is an illicit quantifier shift/scope inversion: the premise’s witness m may depend on n, whereas the conclusion moves ∃m outside ∀n and requires one uniform witness. A choice principle would yield a function f with f(n)>n (for example, f(n)=n+1), not a fixed natural number m. If m were allowed to be a function, or an extended element such as ∞ outside ℕ, that would be a different claim and would not establish the stated natural-number conclusion.

Correction: replace the conclusion with ∀n∈ℕ ∃m∈ℕ (m>n), witnessed by m=n+1. Equivalently, every finite subset S⊆ℕ has an upper bound max(S)+1 in ℕ, but ℕ itself has no upper bound in ℕ.
